domains.name: World — Conditions & Possibilities
domains.definition: Engagement with the facticity of being in the world and the practical question of claiming one's place amid conditions and possibilities.

existential_needs.name: Protection / Acceptance
existential_needs.justification_quote: “This demands three things: protection, space and support.—Do I enjoy protection, acceptance, do I feel at home somewhere?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Space
existential_needs.justification_quote: “This demands three things: protection, space and support… Do I have enough space for being there?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Support
existential_needs.justification_quote: “This demands three things: protection, space and support.—Where do I find support in my life?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Acceptance & Endurance (Active part)
existential_needs.justification_quote: “My active part… is to accept the positive sides and to endure the negative sides… To accept means to be ready to occupy the space, to rely on the support and to trust the protection; in short ‘to be there’ and not to flee. To endure means the force to let be whatever is difficult…”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

positive_indicators.justification_quote: “But if I do have these three things, I will be able to feel trust in the world and confidence in myself, maybe even faith in God. The sum of these experiences of trust is the fundamental trust…”
positive_indicators.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “If this is not the case, the result will be restlessness, insecurity and fear.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions.justification_quote: “If this is not the case, psychodynamics takes over the guidance in the form of coping reactions, which are to secure life.”
coping_reactions.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

inclusion_criteria: Statements about feeling safe/unsafe, belonging, room to exist, external supports/barriers.
Narratives of accepting or enduring immutable conditions to take up space in life.
exclusion_criteria: Purely emotional liking of life without reference to safety/space/support (code under FM2).
Identity/values-focused content without conditions of being (code under FM3).

subthemes.name: Claiming a Place
subthemes.justification_quote: “Can I claim my place in this world under the conditions and with the possibilities I have?”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

subthemes.name: Letting-be / Toleration
subthemes.justification_quote: “Man procures himself the space he needs with his ability to tolerate and to accept conditions.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “Each fundamental motivation has four types of coping reactions: the basic reaction type – here this would be avoidance or flight…”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “…the paradoxical reaction type or activism – here this would be overactivity like fighting bacteria by compulsive washing;”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “…the third type of coping reaction is a specific aggression… – here it would be a destructive aggression such as hate;”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “…the last type of coping reaction is a reflex of freezing, of death imitation with paralysis – here denial or pretending to be non-existent.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

notes.note: Emphasize ontological stance of 'being-in-the-world' and the will to existence (yes/no to world) as FM1 correlates.
notes.justification_quote: “This 'being-in-the-world'… is the fundamental state man finds himself in… In the theory of motivation its correlate is the will to existence, with its yes or no to the world.”
notes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

domains.name: Life — Relationships & Emotions
domains.primary_question: “I am alive—do I like this fact?”
domains.definition: Relational and emotional engagement that gives depth and value to existence through time, closeness, and communal ties.

existential_needs.name: Relationship
existential_needs.justification_quote: “In order to seize my life, to love it, I need three things: relationship, time and closeness.”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Time
existential_needs.justification_quote: “Do I take time for valuable things, worthy to spend my time for? To take time for something means to give away a part of one’s life while spending it with someone or something.”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Closeness
existential_needs.justification_quote: “Can I feel close and maintain closeness to things, plants, animals and people? Can I admit the closeness of someone else?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Consent to feeling / being touched
existential_needs.justification_quote: “If life is to make me move freely, my consent to being touched (to feeling) is necessary.”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

positive_indicators.indicator: Harmony with world/self; depth of life; fundamental value
positive_indicators.justification_quote: “If these three conditions are fulfilled, I experience myself as being in harmony with the world and with myself, and I can sense the depth of life… The sum of these experiences… represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.”
positive_indicators.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

positive_indicators.indicator: Fundamental value as yardstick of worth
positive_indicators.justification_quote: “These experiences form the fundamental value… represents our yardstick for anything we might feel to be of worth.”
positive_indicators.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “If relationships, closeness and time are lacking, longing will arise, then coldness and finally depression.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

risk_markers_if_unmet.marker: Existential vacuum due to lack of relations; social symptoms (addiction, alcoholism, vandalism, emigration, higher suicide rates)
risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “Besides loss of value and lack of orientation in work, lack of relations is another phenomenon causing the existential vacuum… manifesting itself more and more in drug-addiction, alcoholism, vandalism, emigration from society and higher suicide rates.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

inclusion_criteria: Accounts of investing time in people/things, seeking closeness, turning toward/away in grief or love.
Descriptions of emotional resonance (being touched) in relationships or activities.
exclusion_criteria: Safety/space/support concerns without relational content (code under FM1).
Identity/ethical self-affirmation without felt relatedness (code under FM3).

subthemes.name: Turning Toward / Engagement
code_examples: Grieving a loss by turning to it
subthemes.justification_quote: “I seize life… when I turn to other people… If I turn to a loss, grief arises.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

subthemes.name: Pathic Dimension of Life
subthemes.justification_quote: “It has a ‘pathic dimension’… Being alive means to cry and to laugh… The amplitude of emotionality is equal in both directions.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

subthemes.name: Grief as Turning-Toward Loss
code_examples: Letting grief arise by turning toward it
subthemes.justification_quote: “If I turn toward a loss, grief arises.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “The basic coping reaction on this level is regression.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “The activism here is overprotection or achievement, typical forms of combating evil;”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.type: Typical aggression: fury/rage to agitate the other
coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “the typical aggression is fury, rage which does not lead to destruction, but wants to agitate the other person with the impulse to obtain or to improve the relationship.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “Resignation reaction of feigned death paralyzed half-way.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

domains.name: Person — Uniqueness & Conscience
domains.primary_question: “I am myself—may I be like this?”
domains.definition: Identity, autonomy, and ethical self-affirmation grounded in being seen, treated justly, and appreciated.

existential_needs.name: Attention (being seen; boundaries respected)
existential_needs.justification_quote: “In order to succeed here, it is necessary to have experienced three things: attention, justice and appreciation.—…by whom am I seen? Who considers my uniqueness and respects my boundaries?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Justice
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Appreciation
existential_needs.justification_quote: “For what am I appreciated—for what can I appreciate myself?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Saying yes to oneself; encounter and regret
existential_needs.justification_quote: “I also have to say ‘yes to myself.’… Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude.”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

positive_indicators.indicator: Authenticity, relief, self-respect; self-esteem as core worth
positive_indicators.justification_quote: “If… these experiences have been made, I will find myself; find my authenticity, my relief and my self-respect… The sum of these experiences builds one’s own worth… the self-esteem.”
positive_indicators.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “If these experiences are missing, solitude will be the result, hysteria as well as a need to hide behind the shame.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

inclusion_criteria: Statements about being seen/respected, boundary-setting, deservingness, right-to-be.
Reflections on authenticity, conscience, regret, or standing by oneself.
exclusion_criteria: Meaning-making and future-directed contribution (code under FM4).
Purely relational warmth/time/closeness without identity concerns (code under FM2).

subthemes.name: Boundarying & Encounter
subthemes.justification_quote: “to look at other people, to encounter them and, at the same time, to demarcate myself and to stand by my own, but to refuse whatever does not correspond to me.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

subthemes.name: Encounter & Regret as safeguards of authenticity
subthemes.justification_quote: “Encounter and regret are the two means by which we can live our authenticity without ending up in solitude… Thus, I participate in my self-appreciation, attain my self-acceptance.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

subthemes.name: Conscience as Sinn-Organ (organ to find meaning)
code_examples: Referencing an inner sense of rightness/fit
Appeals to conscience when deciding authenticity
subthemes.justification_quote: “conscience… therefore also calls the ‘organ to find meaning’ (Sinn-Organ).”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “The coping reactions of this motivation are: distancing oneself as the basic reaction,”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “…stubborn insistence and leading a functional life as form of activism.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “The typical aggressive reaction consists in indignation, annoyance – anger, reproach.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.type: Freezing: dissociation; splitting emotion and cognition
coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “The freezing type of reaction at this level are dissociation of the bodily integrity, dividing and splitting of emotion and cognition.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

notes.note: Link personal responsibility and justification to right-to-be amidst social structure.
notes.justification_quote: “present and future effects on life by what has been done (responsibility)… the right to live amidst all of life's relations, especially the social structure (justification).”
notes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

domains.name: Meaning — Becoming, Future & Commitment
domains.primary_question: “I am there—for what is it good?”
domains.definition: Orientation toward valuable, realistic possibilities in a broader context, calling for dedication and responsible action.

existential_needs.name: Field of Activity (place to be needed/productive)
existential_needs.justification_quote: “For this, three things are necessary: a field of activity, a structural context and a value to be realized in the future.—is there a place where I feel needed, where I can be productive?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Structural Context (larger orientation)
existential_needs.justification_quote: “Do I see and experience myself in a larger context that provides structure and orientation to my life?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Future Value to Realize
existential_needs.justification_quote: “Is there anything that should still be realized in my life?”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Phenomenological Openness (attitude)
existential_needs.justification_quote: “This attitude of openness represents the existential access to meaning in life: ‘What does this hour want from me, how shall I respond?’”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

existential_needs.name: Meaning as most valuable realistic possibility
existential_needs.justification_quote: “[Meaning is] ‘the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself.’”
existential_needs.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

positive_indicators.indicator: Dedication, action, sense of fulfillment; religious belief
positive_indicators.justification_quote: “If… these conditions are met, I will be capable of dedication and action and, finally, of my own form of religious belief… adds up to the meaning of life and leads to a sense of fulfillment.”
positive_indicators.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “If this is not the case, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and frequently addiction.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

risk_markers_if_unmet.justification_quote: “If I cannot answer these questions in the affirmative, the result will be a feeling of emptiness, frustration, even despair and may frequently result in addiction or suicidal tendencies.”
risk_markers_if_unmet.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

inclusion_criteria: Testimony about contributions, callings, responsibilities, decisions toward valued possibilities.
Situational appraisals of ‘what is asked of me now’ and commitments to future-oriented values.
Mentions of choosing the best possibility oriented by the true (facts), the valuable (good), and the right (responsible relations).
exclusion_criteria: Identity/entitlement content without future-oriented commitment (code under FM3).

subthemes.name: Answering the Situation’s Call
code_examples: What does this hour want from me?
subthemes.justification_quote: “My active part… is to bring myself into agreement with the situation, to examine whether what I am doing is really a good thing: for others, for myself, for the future, for my environment.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2011). The Existential Fundamental Motivations Structuring the Motivational Process. In D. A. Leontiev (Ed.), Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Publishers. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

subthemes.name: Self-Transcendence (moving beyond oneself)
subthemes.justification_quote: “We have to transcend ourselves, if we want to find fulfillment in life and to be fertile. Without this self-transcendence… we are condemned to a life of loneliness and triviality.”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

subthemes.name: Appellative Call of the Situation
subthemes.justification_quote: “meaning is… always appellative by its character of challenge… with its typical call to ‘do something with me!’”
subthemes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

notes.note: Distinguish existential meaning (most valuable realistic possibility now) from ontological meaning (overall meaning not dependent on me).
notes.justification_quote: “Existential meaning is therefore what is possible here and now… Apart from this existential meaning we may also consider an ontological meaning… which does not depend on me.”
notes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

notes.note: Existential vs. ontological meaning distinction reiterated.
notes.justification_quote: “Besides this existential meaning there is an ontological meaning… which does not depend on me.”
notes.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

notes.note: Sequence for finding meaning: reality/facts → valuation → decision/commitment (will to act).
notes.justification_quote: “The seeker of meaning first looks for reality… Perception is followed by an order of valuations… at the third step… enters a personal relation by making a decision.”
notes.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “If man fails systematically to reach meaning, his coping reactions will be a provisional attitude towards life as basic reaction, together with a ‘planless, day-to-day attitude toward life’…”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.type: Activism: collective thinking; idealisation and fanaticism
coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “…and ‘collective thinking’…, idealisation and fanaticism as main forms of activism,”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

coping_reactions_detailed.type: Freezing: fatalism, loss of interest, apathy, nihilism
coping_reactions_detailed.justification_quote: “Fatalism…, loss of interest, apathy and probably nihilism can be seen as forms of freezing reactions.”
coping_reactions_detailed.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

definitions.label: Meaning definition (existential)
definitions.justification_quote: “We define meaning as ‘the most valuable, realistic possibility of the given situation, for which I feel I should decide myself’.”
definitions.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

global_coding_notes.note: Use FM1–FM4 as primary domains. Code subthemes only if anchored in verbatim testimony that fits the LM source quotes. When in doubt, prioritize the participant’s expressed question (can I be? do I like life? may I be myself? for what is it good?).
Do not infer content beyond direct quotes supported by the provided sources. Expand this codebook only with additional user-provided academic materials.
Attend to dialogical cues (being called, challenged, touched) as antecedents of coded actions/decisions.
global_coding_notes.justification_quote: “What a situation 'pro-'vokes in us is indicative of… situational meaning… Being provoked means being called.”
global_coding_notes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

global_coding_notes.note: Operationalize coder judgments by checking for the three steps: recognition of value, harmonization with inner reality, and inner consent.
global_coding_notes.justification_quote: “This model… helps to distinguish three steps within the motivational process: 1. Recognizing… 2. Harmonizing… 3. Giving inner consent…”
global_coding_notes.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

motivational_process.summary: Existential-dialogical view: motivation begins with provocation/call in vis-à-vis and unfolds through three steps—recognizing situational value, harmonizing with inner reality, and giving inner consent to act.

justifications.point: Provocation/call as starting point for any motivation
justifications.quote: “Being provoked means being called. This provocation is the starting point for any motivation.”
justifications.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

justifications.quote: “1. Recognizing something in its worth or value… 2. Harmonizing… with our inner reality… 3. Giving inner consent to one’s own active involvement.”
justifications.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

justifications.quote: “Motivation is understood as engaging in that continuous flow which is established by nature between the person and his world. They are inseparably connected and interrelated, in uninterrupted reciprocal action.”
justifications.citation: Längle, A. (2003). The Art of Involving the Person – Fundamental Existential Motivations as the Structure of the Motivational Process. European Psychotherapy, 4(1), 25–36.

existential_paradigm.quote: “Existence can be seen as a continuous dialogue (preoccupation) with these themes which form the foundation of a fulfilled life.”
existential_paradigm.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

questioned_by_life.quote: “We are ‘questioned, questioned by life’ … ‘What are you going to do with it?’ – How will you relate to them?”
questioned_by_life.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

four_cornerstones.quote: “Human existence is based on these fundamental realities – they are the four cornerstones of existence…: • the world in its factuality and potentiality • life with its network of relationships and its feelings • being oneself as a unique, autonomous person • the future shaped by oneself = development through one’s activities.”
four_cornerstones.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

inner_consent_definition.quote: “The key for a fulfilling existence [is] finding a way of living with inner consent to what we do… contacting the deepest feelings… If these deepest and freest emotions correspond… then we live with inner consent.”
inner_consent_definition.citation: Längle, A. (2002). Existential fundamental motivation. In Motivation, Consciousness and Self-Regulation (pp. 27–42). Nova Science Pub Inc. https://laengle.info/userfile/doc/FM-+-motivation---Leontev-Mosc-2002-2011-publ.pdf

acceptance_criterion_personal_evidence.quote: “Experience shows that meaning can only be accepted when it has passed the 'needle's eye of personal evidence'….”
acceptance_criterion_personal_evidence.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

found_not_invented.quote: “the meaning of life cannot be invented, but must be found.”
found_not_invented.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

objective.quote: “Firstly it is objective ‘on the basis of its situational reference’.”
objective.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

relative.quote: “Secondly, meaning is relative, with regard to the person it is relating to, as well as to further linkages of the situation itself.”
relative.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

subjective.quote: “Thirdly, it is subjective, in that it can only be recognised and realised by the person involved in the respective situation.”
subjective.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

appellative.quote: “Beyond these characteristics… meaning is, fourthly, always appellative by its character of challenge… with its typical call to ‘do something with me!’”
appellative.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

ontological.quote: “The question of meaning on the ontological level is a question to the ground out of which things are and out of which man himself is.”
ontological.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

axiological.quote: “Man… continually faces the axiological question of meaning: ‘What is good about it?’, ‘What is it good for?’”
axiological.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306

existential.quote: “The things that are there continually face him… with the question: ‘What are you doing to do with it?’ This is the existential question of meaning.”
existential.citation: Längle, A. (1992). What Are We Looking for When We Search for Meaning? Ultimate Reality and Meaning, 15(4), 306–314. https://doi.org/10.3138/uram.15.4.306
